## Background

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease. Before a vaccine became
available in the United States in 1963, it caused on the order of hundreds of
thousands of reported cases per year, with epidemics every two to three years.
This report uses the **Project Tycho** weekly U.S. notifiable-disease
surveillance dataset to (1) describe how measles incidence changed over time
and across states, and (2) examine its relationship to childhood measles
immunization coverage.

> **Data source.** Project Tycho, University of Pittsburgh —
> <https://www.tycho.pitt.edu>. The file
> `data/ProjectTycho_Level2_v1.1.0.csv` is **not** committed to this
> repository (see `data/README.md` for how to obtain it). All paths below are
> relative to this `.Rmd`, so the analysis runs on any machine once the file
> is in place.

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)   # dplyr, ggplot2, readr, tidyr, ...
library(lubridate)   # date parsing
library(usmap)       # plot_usmap(), fips()
library(patchwork)   # combining ggplots
library(modelr)      # add_predictions(), add_residuals(), data_grid()
```

## Loading and preparing the data

We read the full surveillance table, then keep only measles records, parse the
date columns, and sort chronologically. Instead of printing the entire data
frame after every step (which bloated the original notebook to several MB), we
use `glimpse()` for a compact overview.

```{r load-data}
data_tycho <- read_csv("data/ProjectTycho_Level2_v1.1.0.csv")
glimpse(data_tycho)
```

```{r prepare-measles}
us_measles <- data_tycho %>%
  filter(disease == "MEASLES") %>%
  mutate(
    from_date = ymd(from_date),
    to_date   = ymd(to_date)
  ) %>%
  arrange(from_date)

glimpse(us_measles)
```

## Geographic distribution: cases per state

We aggregate total reported cases by state and join the FIPS codes that
`usmap` needs to draw the choropleth.

```{r cases-per-state}
cases_per_state <- us_measles %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarize(cases = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(fips = as.numeric(fips(state))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(fips)) %>%
  mutate(values = cases)   # `values` is the column plot_usmap() expects

head(cases_per_state, 10)
```

```{r map, fig.height=5}
plot_usmap(data = cases_per_state, values = "values") +
  scale_fill_continuous(
    low = "#ebf059", high = "#f05959",
    name = "Cases", label = scales::comma
  ) +
  labs(title = "Total reported measles cases per state") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

A handful of large, populous states (e.g. New York, California, Texas)
dominate the cumulative counts, which is expected for a population-driven
infectious disease.

```{r bar-state, fig.height=6}
cases_per_state %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(state, -cases), y = cases)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4682B4") +                       # single colour: the
  labs(                                              # original mapped fill to
    title = "Total measles cases by state",          # `state`, producing a
    x = "State", y = "Cases"                         # 50-key legend that
  ) +                                                # carried no information
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

## Trend over time: cases per year

```{r cases-per-year}
cases_per_year <- us_measles %>%
  group_by(year = year(from_date)) %>%
  summarize(cases = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

tail(cases_per_year, 10)
```

```{r year-bar}
ggplot(cases_per_year, aes(x = year, y = cases)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4682B4") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Reported measles cases per year",
       x = "Year", y = "Cases")
```

The single most informative view of the vaccine's impact is the full annual
time series with the 1963 licensing date marked. Cases fall steeply within a
few years of vaccine introduction.

```{r full-timeline}
ggplot(cases_per_year, aes(x = year, y = cases)) +
  geom_line(color = "#08519c") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1963, linetype = "dashed", color = "#d62728") +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 1963, y = max(cases_per_year$cases, na.rm = TRUE),
    label = " Vaccine licensed (1963)", hjust = 0, color = "#d62728"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "U.S. measles cases per year, with vaccine introduction",
       x = "Year", y = "Reported cases")
```

## Immunization coverage, 1981–2001

> **Provenance note.** The immunization-coverage figures below (percentage of
> children immunized against measles) were transcribed manually. Replace the
> placeholder with the exact citation — e.g. World Bank / WHO–UNICEF estimates
> — and ideally read them from a CSV in `data/` so the numbers are auditable
> rather than hard-coded. The original notebook also loaded a World Bank
> coverage spreadsheet via an intermediate `write.csv()` / `read.csv()` step
> that wrote one filename and read another; that detour is removed here in
> favour of this single explicit table.

```{r vaccination-rate}
vaccination_rate <- tribble(
  ~year, ~immunization_rate,
  1981, 97, 1982, 97, 1983, 98, 1984, 98, 1985, 97,
  1986, 97, 1987, 82, 1988, 98, 1989, 94, 1990, 90,
  1991, 87, 1992, 83, 1993, 84, 1994, 89, 1995, 88,
  1996, 91, 1997, 91, 1998, 92, 1999, 92, 2000, 91, 2001, 91
)

vaccination_rate
```

```{r cases-vs-coverage}
cases_recent <- cases_per_year %>%
  filter(year >= 1981, year <= 2001)

p_cases <- ggplot(cases_recent, aes(year, cases)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#9ecae1") +
  geom_line(color = "#08519c") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Measles cases, 1981–2001", x = "Year", y = "Cases")

p_vacc <- ggplot(vaccination_rate, aes(year, immunization_rate)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#a1d99b") +
  geom_line(color = "#006d2c") +
  labs(title = "Measles immunization rate, 1981–2001",
       x = "Year", y = "Immunization rate (%)")

p_cases / p_vacc + plot_layout(heights = c(3, 1))
```

## Relationship between coverage and cases

We join the two series **by year** so that each case count is matched to the
coverage value for the same year. (The original code built two separately
filtered vectors and correlated them positionally, which only gives the right
answer if the two filters happen to produce identically ordered, equal-length
vectors — a fragile assumption.)

```{r aligned}
aligned <- cases_per_year %>%
  inner_join(vaccination_rate, by = "year")

aligned
```

```{r correlation}
cor.test(aligned$cases, aligned$immunization_rate)
```

```{r linear-model}
model <- lm(cases ~ immunization_rate, data = aligned)
summary(model)
```

```{r model-fit}
grid <- aligned %>%
  data_grid(immunization_rate) %>%
  add_predictions(model)

ggplot(aligned, aes(immunization_rate, cases)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred), data = grid, color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Immunization rate (%)", y = "Cases",
       title = "Cases vs. immunization rate (1981–2001)")
```

```{r residuals}
aligned %>%
  add_residuals(model) %>%
  ggplot(aes(resid)) +
  geom_freqpoly(bins = 10) +
  labs(title = "Model residuals", x = "Residual", y = "Count")
```

> **Statistical caveat.** Restricting this analysis to 1981–2001 keeps every
> observation within the vaccination era, which is deliberate. If you instead
> regress cases on coverage across the *whole* record — mixing pre-vaccine
> years (0% coverage, very high case counts) with post-vaccine years (high
> coverage, low counts) — you get a very strong negative correlation, but that
> number is largely an artefact of the era split (a time confound), not
> evidence of a clean dose–response relationship. The honest evidence for the
> vaccine's effect is the abrupt drop visible in the full annual time series
> above, not a single correlation coefficient.

## Conclusion

The data tell a clear public-health story: U.S. measles incidence collapsed in
the years following the 1963 introduction of the vaccine, and remained low
while immunization coverage stayed high. The vaccine has prevented an enormous
number of cases. The corollary is that sustained high coverage matters — if
vaccination rates fall (for example in the aftermath of pandemic disruption),
the same data give good reason to expect measles to resurge.
